en: The Commentary on the *Nyāyapraveśa* composed by the master Haribhadrasūri.
Homage to the glorious Omniscient One!
Having prostrated before the Lord of Jinas, the teacher of right knowledge,
I compose this clear-meaning commentary on the *Nyāyapraveśaka*.
Although it has been composed both extensively and in brief by those of excellent wisdom, I,
though lacking such wisdom, have done so out of compassion for sentient beings who prefer concise teachings.
And therein:
proof and refutation, along with their fallacies, are for the sake of communicating with others;
whereas perception and inference, along with their fallacies, are for the sake of one's own communication.
This is the very verse beginning with those words. [An objection] asks: "Why is this presented at the beginning?
It is said in reply:

In this world, those who act with prior deliberation do not engage in anything that is devoid of a purpose and so forth; therefore, [this work] is commenced as a treatise called the *Nyāyapraveśaka* for the sake of inducing the engagement of discerning persons by demonstrating the purpose and other elements of the treatise under discussion, and also for the sake of refuting the reasons for non-engagement that might be imagined by others at the time the meaning of the treatise is being explained.
When this has been stated, an opponent might indeed argue as follows: "This [treatise] should not be commenced because it is devoid of a purpose, like the speech of a madman."
Likewise, because it lacks a subject matter to be expressed, it is like an examination of a crow’s teeth;
likewise, because it is incoherent, it is like such sentences as "ten pomegranates, six cakes, a pot, a goat-skin, a lump of meat, a lake, an ant.

Therefore, at the outset, this verse is presented for the purpose of demonstrating the utility [of the treatise] and so forth, in order to point out the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of these aforementioned reasons.
And this [verse] demonstrates the subject matter and the purpose directly, while the relationship [between them] is shown by implication.
How this is so, we shall demonstrate by providing a brief explanation in this very manner for the sake of easy comprehension.
And commentary consists in the connection of words and sentences. As it has been said:

"From what source can there be a correct understanding of the meaning of treatises, chapters, and so forth, if one sets aside commentary? And that [commentary] has been described by those who know reality as pertaining to words and sentences."

In this regard as well, since a sentence consists of a collection of words, it is logical that one first proceeds by determining the meaning of the individual words; and since that [determination] is preceded by the division of words, the division of the words follows:

"Proof and refutation, along with their fallacies, are for the sake of another's cognition; perception and inference, along with their fallacies, are for the sake of one's own cognition"—these are the words.
Now the meaning of the term is stated:
it is called a *sādhana* because by means of it something is established (*sādhyate*), or it is an establishment (*siddhi*), or it establishes (*sādhayati*).
And that consists of the collection of statements concerning the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth.
And it will be said:
"The statements of the thesis and so forth constitute the proof;
and its object is the locus (dharmin) as qualified by the property (dharma)."
Likewise, it is called *dūṣaṇa* (refutation) because one is corrupted by it, or because it corrupts;
and that is indeed a collection of statements consisting in the pointing out of defects in the proof (*sādhana*).
And he will state later: "Refutations are the pointing out of defects in the proof."

And its object is a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*), not a correct proof (*samyaksādhana*), because it is impossible to refute that [latter]. But will it not be stated that "refutations (*dūṣaṇa*) are the pointing out of defects in a proof"? How then is this [to be understood]? It is said:
"There is no fault because the term 'proof' is applied metaphorically to what is merely a fallacious proof due to some slight similarity"—this we shall examine in that very place.
The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction;
the particle "eva" (only/just) is used for restriction.

And we shall demonstrate that this is for the purpose of excluding connection with anything else. Likewise, appearance (*ābhāsa*) is the act of appearing; that which exists together with appearance is "with appearance" (*sābhāsam*).
The term "with fallacy" (sābhāsa) is connected to each [term] individually:
proof with fallacy (sādhanābhāsa) and refutation with fallacy (dūṣaṇābhāsa). Among these, the fallacy of proof consists of fallacious theses (pakṣābhāsa) and so forth.
And he will say:
"Even that which is intended to be proven is a fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*) if it contradicts perception and so forth," and so on;
and "fallacious refutations (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*) are the pointing out of non-existent faults in the proof."
And he will further state that the pointing out of faults in proving what is unreal constitutes fallacious refutations.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the cognition of others" (*parasaṃvide*): here, "others" refers to the judges; "cognition" (*saṃvit*) means awareness or understanding.

The "cognition of others" is *parasaṃvit*; [the compound means] for that cognition of others, that is, for the purpose of making others understand. This is the dative case used in the sense of "for the sake of" (*tādarthye*).
"Just as wood for a sacrificial post"—
this is the meaning of the term.

This is the meaning of the statement: it is only proof and refutation, along with their fallacious counterparts, that lead to the cognition of another— that is, the awakening of another— rather than perception and inference,
because the fruit of those two is the cognition of another.
Just as when Pārtha himself is the archer, while Pārtha is wielding the bow, who else could be said to be wielding the bow?

Regarding the term *pratyakṣa*, *akṣa* means the sense faculty (*indriya*). Consequently, *pratyakṣa* means that which has gone toward the sense faculty; the meaning is that it has gone toward the sense faculty by way of being its effect.
And this [author] will state later: "Perception is free from conceptual construction," and so forth.
Likewise, *māna* means that by which something is measured; the meaning is that it is delimited.
The prefix *anu* has the sense of "subsequent. Inference (*anumāna*) is subsequent cognition;
that is to say, it is preceded by the apprehension of the property in the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and the recollection of the [invariable] relation.
And he will say: "Inference is the cognition of the inferable (liṅgin) from a mark (liṅga) possessing three characteristics.
The word "and" (ca) is as before.
[The phrase] "with its fallacies," and so forth, follows.
And he will state: "Conceptual cognition regarding a different object is pseudo-perception," and so forth;
likewise, "Cognition preceded by a fallacious reason is pseudo-inference," and so forth.
The word *tu* (but/however) has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*.
And we shall demonstrate that this [term] is indeed a restrictive particle (avadhāraṇa).
Regarding the term *ātmasaṃvid*:
that which extends (*atatīti*) is the self (*ātman*), namely the living being (*jīva*);
*saṃvit* is the act of cognizing (*saṃvedanam*).
"Self-cognition" (*ātmasaṃvit*) means cognition of the self;
it is for the sake of that self-cognition, that is, for the realization of the self.
And here, "self" is understood as being of the nature of the continuum of mind and mental factors (*cittacaittasaṃtāna*), and not as the eternal entity and so forth imagined by others.
This is because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes it;
such is the meaning of the term.
This is the meaning of the sentence:

perception and inference, along with their fallacious counterparts (*sābhāsa*), are themselves the self-cognitions for the sake of realizing the Self; they are not the means of proof (*sādhana*) or refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), because those two have self-cognition as their fruit.

[The opponent] says: "But surely, since the means of proof is in reality nothing other than inference, then once it has been stated that 'inference' and so forth, it is not appropriate to mention the 'means of proof,' or else, given what was previously stated, it is not appropriate to mention 'inference.'"
This is not a fault,
because it is stated by distinguishing between inference for oneself and inference for others;
therein, inference for others is the means of proof (*sādhana*), whereas this [present case] is inference for oneself.
But another says:
"At the outset, the statement of proof and refutation is improper, because their application must be preceded by perception and inference.
It is replied:

Even though the commencement of the treatise is preceded by that [the purpose], it is presented at the beginning because the primary aim is the cognition of others (*parasaṃvit*), and because both proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) have that as their fruit due to their close proximity [to the goal].
Others hold that this is for the purpose of demonstrating the principle that what is composed for the sake of others is [ultimately] for one's own sake (*svārtha*).
Enough with this digression;
let us return to the subject at hand.
And here, the eight categories beginning with the means of proof (sādhana) are stated as the subject matter;
the purpose, consisting of the realization of others and the realization of oneself, is likewise mentioned, while the relationship [between them] is understood through implication alone.
And that relationship is characterized by the nature of cause and effect.
The cause is the very treatise that has taken the form of words;
the effect, however, is the thorough comprehension of the meaning of that treatise.
For it is in this way that the genitive case, characterized by its relation, is used [to express] "this is the effect of that."

He says: "If this is so, then because the cognition of another and the cognition of oneself are separated by the thorough understanding of the meaning of the treatise's subject matter, they would be purposeless. [The author replies: No, for it is precisely that which is separated which is intended to be expressed. [The opponent asks: For what purpose is that which is separated intended to be expressed?
It is said:
for the purpose of demonstrating the preeminence of each successive objective;
and thus, in this context, the unsurpassed objective is precisely the attainment of the supreme state.

And so it has been said: "By thoroughly understanding the correct method, those who discern what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted take up that which is to be adopted and proceed to the supreme goal."
He asks: "If this is so, why has this very [teaching] not been presented here as the unsurpassed?
It is said:
Because, with reference to a group of disciples who have not yet attained proficiency, it would be useless to present it at the very outset.
But another says:
"This purpose has been stated here for the listeners; however, it must be stated what the purpose is for the author.
It is replied:
This very same [benefit] is divided into immediate and remote types. First, the immediate is the assistance rendered to sentient beings;
the remote, however, is the attainment of the supreme destination itself.
And so it has been said:
"He who bestows favor upon sentient beings by teaching the correct method to those who are outside the method shall, before long, attain Śiva."
Enough with further elaboration.
Thus is the compendium of the treatise.
The word "iti" indicates completion;
it means "just this much."

That by which reality (*tattva*) is taught is precisely what is meant here by "treatise" (*śāstra*); it is so called because it is sought after (*arthyate*). The meaning of the treatise is the "meaning of the treatise" (*śāstrārtha*).
Its "compendium" (saṃgraha) is the compendium of the meaning of the treatise;
"compilation" (saṃgrahaṇa) means a compendium.
The meaning is that this alone is the summary of the subject matter of the authoritative treatise under consideration.
And according to the tradition of the elders, this is because, although it is a short treatise, it teaches the principles that pervade the entire universe.
In this regard, since the explanation follows the order of the enumeration, he says the following in order to determine the essential nature of the proof (*sādhana*).
In that context, the statements regarding the thesis and so forth constitute the proof (*sādhana*). The word "therein" (*tatra*) has the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*);
it means that among those [elements] such as the proof and so on, the proof is first selected.
And it is held that specification (*nirdhāraṇa*) is based on genus, quality, or action.
In this context, specification by means of a quality occurs when something is specified by its quality as being an instrument;
for example, a cow is distinguished from a herd of cows by the quality of being rich in milk.
That which is cooked (pacyate) is a "side" (pakṣaḥ). The root *pac* means "to manifest.
That object which is cooked—that is, manifested—is the "side."
The meaning is "the probandum" (*sādhya*). And that is the locus (*dharmin*) as qualified by its property (*dharma*).
"Those whose first is the thesis" (*pakṣādayaḥ*) refers to those things beginning with the thesis.

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, and it is one that involves the recognition of the quality (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*). Among these, an example of one involving the recognition of the quality is "long-eared" (*lambakarṇa*) and so forth.
He whose ears are long is "lambakarṇaḥ";
the meaning is that having long ears is a quality belonging to him alone.
An example of a term where the qualities are not included in the cognition (atadguṇasaṃvijñāna) is "a field such as a mountain," and so forth.
That field which has mountains and so forth as its beginning is called "mountainous" (*parvatādika*) and so on.
A mountain is not a quality of the field; what then? [It is the locus of that field.]
The intention is that this is merely an illustration.
Here, it should be understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities [of the members] are included (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*),
such as "a field with mountains and so forth" or "a forest with rivers and so forth."
It is not, however, like [the case of] "long-eared" being a term for the Brahmin and other castes (*varṇa*).
In the expression "propositions such as the thesis (*pakṣa*) are the means of proof," the word "etc. (*ādi*) is intended as an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).
And this is its meaning:
That from which something is taken is an "ādi" (beginning/source), as in the case of "the field beginning with the mountain" (*parvatādikaṃ kṣetram*) and so forth;
it is not, however, that which is not taken, as in the case of "the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇādayo varṇāḥ*) and so forth.
Therefore, this position is well-established: those for whom [the *pakṣa*] is the first are "those beginning with the *pakṣa*" (*pakṣādayaḥ*).
And those reasons and examples characterized by the [two] sides are the arguments; their verbal expressions are the "reasonings" (yuktis).

"What is the means of proof (sādhana)? In this context, when the word *sādhana* has the sense of denoting an instrument—as in "that by which something is proven"—then the statements of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, as characterized by the thesis (*pakṣa*), constitute the means of proof.
For by those [statements], acting as instruments, the intended object is communicated to the mental continuum of another.

Furthermore, when "proof" (*sādhana*) is understood as the accomplishment of an entity— that is, the proof itself— then the proof is simply the knowledge residing in the person being instructed, which is produced by the statements of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth.
This is because the statements of the thesis and so forth are the fruit [of that knowledge],
and [the term "proof"] is applied to the cause by metaphorical designation upon the effect.

Just as one says, "This body of mine is the result of past karma," when the term *sādhana* (means of accomplishment) is used in the sense of the agent who accomplishes, then the statements of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth are intended to be the agent, because they produce knowledge within the continuum of the person being instructed. Thus, in this way, the statements of the thesis and so forth constitute the *sādhana*.
For example: trees [constitute] a forest; elephants and so forth [constitute] an army.
[The opponent] asks: For what purpose is this expressed as a singular designation?

This is for the purpose of demonstrating that the statements regarding the "proponent's position" (*pakṣa*) and so forth are the means of proof (*sādhana*) only when combined. And it has been said by the Master Dignāga: "The singular grammatical designation 'the means of proof' is for the purpose of indicating that the [elements] taken as a whole constitute the means of proof.
Enough of this elaboration.
Thus, the proof has first been stated in general terms.
However, it is not yet known whether this [proof] is a producer (*kāraka*) or a manifester (*vyañjaka*),
since two types of proof are observed.
In this context, the producer (*kāraka*) is [the cause] of the sprout and so forth, such as the seed;
the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is [the cause] of jars and so forth in the dark, such as a lamp.
Therefore, in order to establish its nature as a manifestor, he says:
For it is by means of the statements of the thesis, the reason, and the example that a matter not yet understood by the judges is established.
The explanation of these terms is as follows: it is called a "position" (*pakṣa*) because it is cooked (*pacyate*); it is called a "reason" (*hetu*) because it leads (*hinoti*).
For *hi* means "to go.
All roots meaning "to go" also mean "to know.
Likewise, that which leads a perceived object to its end (*anta*) is called an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*).
And that [example] is of two kinds, distinguished by similarity and dissimilarity.
Consequently, the compound is as follows:
example and example are "the two examples" (dṛṣṭāntau).
The reason (*hetu*) and the examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) are "reasons and examples.
The reasons and examples of the thesis (*pakṣa*) are "the thesis, reasons, and examples. The statements of these are "the statements of the thesis, reasons, and examples."
By those statements of the thesis, the reason, and the example;
the word "hi" (for) has the sense of "because";
the judges (*prāśnika*) are learned men appointed by the question.
[They are] those who know both their own system and the systems of others. And it has been said:

"Those who know their own system and the systems of others, who are of noble birth, who abide by both sides [of the argument], who are patient, and who are engaged in the paths of debate—such arbitrators are said to be equal to a scale."
An object that is unperceived, uncomprehended, and not understood by those judges is being explained.
He asks:
"How can there be any object unperceived by those judges who have been described as such?"
It is said:
it is not the case that [the meaning] is unestablished by virtue of not being accepted as a thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*);
rather, because it falls within the scope of what is incapable of supporting the positions adopted by the proponent and the opponent, the unestablished meaning is thus demonstrated.

But surely, in this case, it ought to be stated by means of the fourth case (*cāturthī*) according to the rule "and by the action" (*kriyayā ca*); for what purpose, then, is the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) used here? [The answer is: the sixth case is used as a residual marker (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*) because there is no intention to express the grammatical factors (*kāraka*). Of which [factors] is it expressed?
By implication, since it is not understood by some and has not been heard by others, it is explained specifically for them.
The word "iti" (thus) has the sense of "therefore.
Because this is so, this proof is a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), because it conveys a meaning that was previously unapprehended, like a lamp.
In the case of difference, [the example is] the seed and so forth.
In that context, it has been stated that the statements regarding the thesis and so forth constitute the proof.
Now, following the principle that "the explanation follows the enumeration," he says [the following] to set forth the definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*):
"In this context, the thesis is a well-known subject (*dharmin*). The method for understanding this is as follows:"

In this context, the word *tatra* (therein) has the sense of specification (*nirdhāraṇa*). And this specification is to be understood by way of qualities such as being a well-known subject (*prasiddhadharmin*) and so forth. "The thesis" (*pakṣa*) is the indication of the definiendum (*lakṣya*).
Regarding the term *dharmin*: "dharmas" refers to properties such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth; that which possesses these is the *dharmin*, such as sound and the like.
To the question "In what way is it established? he says:
That which is intended by oneself as the probandum (sādhya) as being qualified by a well-known qualifier (*prasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*):
therein, "well-known" (*prasiddha*) means that which has been apprehended by both the proponent (*vādin*) and the opponent (*prativādin*) through the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It is called a "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) because one is distinguished (*viśiṣyate*) by means of it.
Distinguished by that [attribute] means distinguished by a well-known qualifier.
The state of being so is "the state of being distinguished by a well-known qualifier.
By means of that state of being distinguished by a well-known qualifier, acting as the logical reason (*hetu*), [the subject] is established.
To this it is replied: In this case, while the established nature of the subject (*dharmin*) is appropriate, that of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), such as impermanence and so forth, is not appropriate,
because it is yet to be proven (*sādhyatvāt*).
Otherwise, because there would be no dispute, the application of a proof would be untenable.
This is not so,
because of a failure to understand the correct meaning.
In this context, the well-known status of the qualifier is not based on that very same subject (dharmin), but rather on another subject such as a jar;
consequently, the aforementioned fault does not arise.
Likewise, by the word "himself" (svayam), the acceptance of an acknowledged tenet (abhyupagama-siddhānta) is intended.

Regarding the phrase "desired as that which is to be proven" (*sādhyatvenepsita*): it is called "the provable" (*sādhya*) because it is to be established (*sādhanīya*), or because it ought to be established (*sādhayitavya*), or because it deserves proof (*sādhanam arhati*).
The state of being such is "provable-ness" (*sādhyatva*).
"By that" means by way of being the probandum (*sādhya*). "Desired" (*īpsita*) means intended, wished for, or accepted; the meaning is that it is pervaded by the desire [to prove it].

And here, since a qualifier functions as an excluder, one should understand that by the phrase "the subject is well-known," the fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*) whose qualifier is unestablished is excluded.

By the phrase "qualified by well-known qualifiers," one should see the exclusion of that whose qualifiers are not well-known; by the word "both," the exclusion of that whose both [qualifiers and qualificand] are not well-known;

and by the word "himself" (svayam), through the inclusion of the tenet established by personal admission (abhyupagama-siddhānta), the exclusion of the tenets established for all systems (sarvatantra-siddhānta), for specific systems (pratitantra-siddhānta), and as contextual conclusions (adhikaraṇa-siddhānta) is to be understood.

In this context, however, the statement regarding the acceptance of a property and its locus (dharma-dharmin) that are well-known in the world, without reliance on a specific treatise, is the "accepted tenet" (abhyupagama-siddhānta); he expresses this by the word "himself" (svayam).

Therefore, when a proponent himself states a proof at that time—even if he states the proof while standing within some treatise, and although the author of that treatise has accepted many properties for that locus—[the tenet remains his own].

"Even so, what has been stated by that preeminent debater— that only that property which this proponent intends to prove at that time is the *sādhya* (the thing to be proven), and nothing else— is indeed consistent.
By the phrase 'as the *sādhya*,' it means precisely as the *sādhya*, and not even as a *sādhana* (the means of proof)."
And by this [definition], the exclusion of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) from being the subject (*pakṣa*) is established.
Furthermore, by the word "intended" (*īpsita*), it is stated that it is not merely what has been verbally expressed;
rather, the subject is pervaded by intention as well.
We shall demonstrate this in the section concerning "the eyes and so forth are for the sake of another.
By this, it is made known that the *pakṣa* (the subject) is the substratum (*dharmin*) as qualified by a property (*dharma*).

Consequently, the meaning is that neither the property alone, nor the substratum alone, nor both independently, nor the relation between them constitutes the *pakṣa*; rather, it is the state of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) between the property and the substratum.

Furthermore, even when the aforementioned definition is satisfied, there would result the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*)—namely, that statements such as "sound is inaudible," which are not contradicted by perception, would also attain the status of being a thesis (*pakṣa*).
To exclude this, he adds the remainder of the sentence: "not contradicted by perception and so forth" (*pratyakṣādyaviruddha*).
This means it must be non-contradictory with respect to perception and the other [means of valid cognition].
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of unmentioned means such as inference is intended;
thus, this should be understood as a completion of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) or an ellipsis (*vākyādhyāhāra*).
To provide an illustration, he says: "For example."
"Is sound impermanent or permanent?"—the phrase "for example" (*tadyathā*) is used for the purpose of presenting an illustration.
In this regard, for a Buddhist and others, sound is impermanent; for a grammarian and others, it is permanent.
The thesis (*pakṣa*) has been stated along with its examples.
Now, wishing to state the reason (*hetu*), he says: "The reason has three characteristics.
In this context, it is called a reason because it leads (*hinoti*) or makes known (*gamayati*) objects qualified by the property one desires to know.
And that [reason] possesses three forms (*trirūpa*).
That which has three forms is "three-formed," meaning it has a triple nature.
Not perceiving the multiplicity within a single entity, the questioner asks: "What, then, is this three-fold form?"
*Kim* is used in the sense of an inquiry;
*punar* is used in the sense of deliberation;
and *trairūpyam* is the state of possessing three forms (*trirūpa*).

Thus, being questioned by the interrogator, the master of the manual (ācārya) states the presence of the reason in the subject (pakṣadharmatva), its existence in similar instances (sapakṣe sattva), and its absolute absence in dissimilar instances (vipakṣe 'sattva). This is the method of understanding it: the property of that which has been designated as the subject is "subject-property" (pakṣadharma); the state of being that is "subject-property-ness" (pakṣadharmatva).
And here, by the word *pakṣa*, the subject (*dharmin*) alone is denoted,
because the term for the whole is applied metaphorically to its part;
this is one form [of the thesis].

Likewise, there is presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*). The similar class has the definition that will be stated later; "presence" in it means existence, which signifies being present in a general sense.
This is the second characteristic.

Likewise, its non-existence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is the third characteristic. The counter-example has the definition that will be stated hereafter; furthermore, its "non-existence" therein means precisely its non-occurrence.
The word *ca* has the meaning of the word *punaḥ*.
And it has already been shown that this [word] serves the purpose of specification (*viśeṣārtha*). He asks: why is there a statement of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) right here?
It is said:
this is for the purpose of demonstrating absolute non-existence in that very [locus]; however, existence even in one part of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is indeed not defective.

And this being so, it is thereby made known that qualities such as "being produced immediately after effort" (prayatnānantarīyakatva) are indeed valid reasons (samyag-hetu), since they are invariably excluded from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) even while pervading only a portion of the similar instances (sapakṣa).

Regarding what was stated as "presence in the similar class" (*sapakṣe sattvam*) and so forth, the disciple, not knowing the essential nature of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), asks: "What, then, is the similar class, and what is the dissimilar class?
This question, however, is established by the very words [of the definition].

This etymological explanation, however, begins with "the property to be proven" (*sādhyadharma*) and so forth. The method for understanding this is as follows: here, by means of metaphorical application (*upacāra-vṛtti*), the state of being the "probandum" (*sādhyatva*) is predicated of the property (*dharma*).
That which is to be proven (*sādhya*) and which is a property (*dharma*) is the "property to be proven" (*sādhyadharma*), such as impermanence and so forth.
Being common (*samāna*) means similar; its state (*bhāva*) is "commonality" (*sāmānya*), that is, similarity.

The "similarity of the property to be proven" (*sādhyadharma-sāmānya*) refers to the commonality between the property to be proven and [the subject] by way of that very property to be proven. An object that is similar by virtue of that [commonality] is the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*). It is called "similar" (*samāna*) because its measure (*māna*) is equal (*sama*) or equivalent (*tulya*).
The meditative cultivation is that which is to be delimited by an equivalent measure;
the object is a jar or the like, but not mere words.
"Equal side" means "similar side" (*sapakṣa*).

Alternatively, by way of metaphorical application (*upacāra-vṛtti*), the status of being the "probandum" (*sādhya*) is attributed to the subject (*dharmin*). Consequently, the "property of the probandum" (*sādhyadharma*) is the property belonging to that which is to be proven.
The remainder is as before. However, the probandum (sādhya) is not used in a figurative sense; the meaning of the term is "the subject (dharmin) as qualified by the property (dharma)."
Now, demonstrating an example that possesses a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), he says:
"For example, when sound is to be proven as impermanent," and so forth.
The phrase "for example" (*tadyathā*) is for the purpose of introducing an illustration.
When sound is to be proven as impermanent, what is it?
A collection of objects such as a jar and so forth is the similar instance (sapakṣa), because of its similarity to the property of impermanence to be proven.
Now, in order to explain the definition of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), he says: "The counter-example is that wherein the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent;
a dissimilar instance (*visadṛśaḥ pakṣaḥ*) is the counter-example (*vipakṣaḥ*)."
He shows its nature by asking "of what kind is it?"— that is, in which object (*artha*) the probandum (*sādhya*) is to be established.

"It does not exist" means it is not found. Furthermore, because the means of proof (*sādhana*) is invariably connected with the probandum (*sādhya*), it is understood that the latter also does not exist. He shows an example:
As for the passage beginning "That which is eternal," etc.: what is meant by "that which is eternal"?
It means that whatever is not impermanent is seen to be uncreated.
"Even that which is produced is not seen [to exist] like space";
for in that case, there is an absence of the probans due to the absence of the probandum.
Now, because the method of restriction is manifold, he says the following while demonstrating it with respect to the property of being present in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) and so forth:
In that context, "the state of being produced" (kṛtakatva) and so forth:
"therein" is as before;
the construction is that the state of being produced, or the state of following immediately after effort (prayatnānantarīyakatva), is the logical reason (hetu) for [proving] impermanence and so on.
In this context, "produced" (*kṛtaka*) means that which is made (*kriyate*).
For an entity (*bhāva*) whose operation depends upon another is called "produced" (*kṛtaka*) with respect to the accomplishment of its own nature (*svabhāva*);
the state of being such is "producibility" (*kṛtakatva*).
Or, it is "being produced immediately after effort.
Effort (*prayatna*) is the activity of one possessing consciousness. That which comes into existence there immediately after that effort is "produced immediately after effort" (*prayatnāntarīya*).
That very thing is "following immediately after effort. Its state is "the quality of following immediately after effort. The word "vā" has the sense of the word "ca" (and).
And that [particle *ca*] is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

The statement of the second reason is: "Even that which is excluded from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) and occurs in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) is a valid reason (*samyaghetu*)," as for example: [the syllogism: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced. In this case, the property of being produced is excluded from the dissimilar instances (such as space) and occurs in only a portion of the similar instances (namely, products like pots, but not in others such as lightning). Thus, it is a valid reason.
Because the phrase "yameva" (whichever one) serves the purpose of indicating perception, it is not faulty.
Furthermore, this reason is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) itself, but not a property belonging exclusively to the subject (*pakṣasyaiva dharmaḥ*),
because the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) has as its sole result the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).

Just as "Caitra is indeed an archer," by which there is the exclusion of the four types of unestablished reasons (*asiddha*) and of the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*); likewise, let there be the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) only in the sense that "Pārtha alone is the archer."
By this, however, there is the exclusion of all nine types of fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa), beginning with the "common" (sādhāraṇa).
He says:
if [the reason] exists only in the similar instances (sapakṣa), then because it is absent elsewhere—in the subject (pakṣa) as well as in other places—its status as a property (dharma) is untenable.
Not so, because there is no restriction of the restriction;
for the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) has already been restricted.
He says:
If this is so, for what purpose is the third restriction, "it does not exist in the counter-example"?
It is said:
it is for the purpose of demonstrating the formal argument (*prayoga*).
And it has been said:
"How indeed might even one form of either positive concomitance (anvaya) or negative concomitance (vyatireka), when stated, imply the second?
Much could be said on this matter, but it is not stated here.
For fear of excessive prolixity, this is merely a guide; by the inclusion of the word "etc.
(*ādi*) in the phrase "the cause in impermanence, etc.," there is the inclusion of suffering and so forth.
Thus has the reason been explained.
Now, wishing to state the example, he says:
"The example," and so forth.
An example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is that which leads one to the end (*anta*) of the meaning seen (*dṛṣṭa*) therein.
The meaning is that only that which is apprehended by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is brought to the state of being established through experience when there is a dispute.
And that [means of valid cognition] is of two kinds;
"dvividha" means that which has two modes (dve vidhe), and that itself is the twofold nature (dvaividhya).
He demonstrates by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) and by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

That which possesses a common property is *sadharmā*; the state of being such is *sādharmya*, and it is by that [means]. That which possesses a discordant property is *vidharmā*; the state of being such is *vaidharmya*, and it is by that [means].
The word "ca" (and) signifies conjunction.
In that context, the phrase "first, by way of similarity" (*sādharmyeṇa tāvat*) is used;
there, the word "tāvat" indicates the sense of sequence.
Regarding the phrase "wherein":
it is demonstrated that the probans (hetu), which possesses the characteristics already stated, exists only in the similar instances (sapakṣa);
that is, its existence—its being present—is demonstrated and established by means of the statement within those similar instances characterized as previously described.
And this [is as follows]:
"Whatever is produced is impermanent, like a jar and so forth"—this is easy to understand. By this, the fallacies of the probans (*sādhana*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are indicated.
By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) as well:
where it is stated that in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), there is necessarily an absence of the reason (*hetvabhāva*).
"Where" (*yatra*) refers to that which is to be expressed.
The probandum, such as impermanence and so forth—in its absence, what happens to the reason, such as "being produced" and so forth?
It is stated that there is indeed an absence; it is demonstrated by means of verbal expression.
And he shows this example:
"That which is eternal is seen to be uncreated, as for instance space"—this is easy to understand.
He says:
For the followers of the Sugata, there is nothing whatsoever that is eternal.
Since such a thing does not exist, how can a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) be cited? By the word "eternal" (nitya), what is meant here is the absence of impermanence (anityatva).
In this context— either in the formal argument (*prayoga*) or in the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—
is it by the word "eternal" (*nitya*) that the absence of non-eternality is expressed?
[That is,] "eternal" means "it does not become non-eternal."
By the term "unproduced" (akṛtaka), the absence of being produced is also expressed;
this is how it functions.
One who does not possess the quality of being produced is "unproduced."
But there is no real entity that is eternal or unconditioned.
Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration:
"Just as the absence of an entity is itself an absence."
The word "yathā" is used in the sense of comparison.
*Bhāva* means existence; the non-existence of that is *bhāvābhāva*. This is what is called "non-existence" (*abhāva*).

But there is no such thing as non-existence (abhāva) that has the nature of a real entity (vastu-svarūpa) distinct from existence (bhāva); thus, it has already been explained in the case of the subject of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika) as well, beginning with the words "here by the word 'eternal'."
The sides and so forth have been described.

The meaning is that the reasons (*hetu*) and examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), together with the thesis (*pakṣa*) which serves as their object, are intended; "of these" refers to the reasons and examples characterized by the thesis.
"Words" refers to those expressive sounds; what [is their function]?
They are the means of proof at the time of communicating with others—that is, at the time of communicating with an opponent.
As he demonstrates through the formal application [of the syllogism]:
"Sound is impermanent" is the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*);
"because it is produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*) is the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmavacana*).

"That which is produced is seen to be impermanent, such as a jar and so forth"—this is the statement of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). "That which is permanent is seen to be unproduced, such as space"—this is the statement of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
This is established by the literal reading of the text.
To this extent, these alone are called the three members;
these alone are the statements of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
"Three" refers to the number.
They are called "members" (avayava). This is another designation used by the ancient masters (pūrvācārya), as it has been stated: "The members are the means of proof (sādhana)."
The proof (*sādhana*) has been explained; now its fallacious counterpart (*tad-ābhāsa*) is being discussed.
In that regard, since the statement of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth constitutes the proof, and because the thesis serves as the primary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), the thesis is mentioned first.
Here too, it is stated that "that which is intended to be proven" and so forth refers precisely to a fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*).
Even though something is desired to be proven, if it contradicts the definition of a thesis, it is a fallacious thesis.

By the word "even" (*api*), it is implied that although it is what one wishes to establish through the desire to prove it, it may also possess other characteristics such as being a well-known subject (*dharmin*) and so on.
What [is it]?
It is that which contradicts perception and so forth.
That which is contradicted is "contradictory" (viruddha).
Perception and the other means of valid cognition have definitions that will be stated hereafter; that which is contradicted or refuted by them is "contradicted by perception and the rest.
What is it?
It is a fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*).
In this context, the "proposition" (*pakṣa*) has the characteristics already described; its "semblance" (*ābhāsa*) is the mere appearance, that is, the mere form.

That which has the semblance of a proposition is a "semblance of a proposition" (*pakṣābhāsa*), meaning it possesses merely the form of a proposition, but is not a correct proposition—this is the sense.
The phrase "tadyathā" (for example) serves the purpose of introducing an illustration.
Regarding the expression "contradicted by direct perception" (*pratyakṣaviruddha*) and so forth:
"direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) refers to that which will have its definition stated below.
In this context, however, by the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), the property (*dharma*) determined by it is intended, according to the maxim of the *śāli*-grain measure (*kuḍava*).
Consequently, through the elision of the well-known words "property" (*dharma*), "contrary to a property established by perception" becomes "contrary to perception" (*pratyakṣaviruddha*).
In the same way, one should contemplate the [terms] "contrary to inference" (*anumānaviruddha*), as well as those contrary to scripture, the world, and one's own statement.

We shall explain the meaning of terms such as "unestablished qualification" (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*) precisely during the examination of examples. For now, he presents the examples. Among them, "contradicted by perception" (*pratyakṣaviruddha*) is the brief statement (*uddeśa*).
For example, "sound is inaudible. Here, "sound" is the subject (*dharmin*),
and "inaudibility" is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
And this [property] being established in that very subject (dharmin) is contradicted by audibility, which is established by perception; thus, it is "contradicted by perception" (*pratyakṣaviruddha*).

[The opponent] says: "Since audibility has the nature of a universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), it is not at all accessible through perception; how then can it be 'contradicted by a property established by perception'?"
To this it is replied:
there is no fault, because since the abstract suffix denotes only the essential nature (svarūpa), it is impossible for it to be a general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
And although much could be said on this point, it is not stated here.
Because the effort would be fruitless, merely for the sake of following the literal syllables.
An example of that which is contradicted by inference (*anumānaviruddha*) is: "A pot is eternal.
Here, the pot is the subject (*dharmin*).

Eternality is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). And that [property] is sublated with respect to that very subject (*dharmin*) by impermanence, which is established through inference. And this is the inference:
A pot is impermanent because its acquisition of self-nature depends upon causes, like a lamp.
Contradiction with scripture (*āgamaviruddha*) is as follows:

when a Vaiśeṣika, having undertaken the acceptance of a thesis by thinking "I am a Vaiśeṣika," asserts the permanence of sound while attempting to prove that "sound is permanent," then it is a contradiction with scripture.
For its eternity is well-established by scripture;

and it has been stated that "the composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by an intelligent being," and "the authority of the sacred tradition [Āmnāya] arises from the word of such a being," and so forth.
An example of that which contradicts worldly consensus (*lokaviruddha*) is as follows:
"A human skull is pure because it is a part of a living being, like a conch shell or mother-of-pearl.
In this case, the human skull is presented as the subject (*dharmin*).
Purity is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
And that very property, while being established, is refuted by means of the purity well-known in the world regarding that same subject (*dharmin*).
Thus he says:
For what purpose is the employment of reasons and examples stated here?
It is for the sake of demonstrating the superior force of worldly convention;
the meaning is that even by means of inference, what is well-established in the world is not sublated.
An example of a contradiction with one's own words is:
"My mother is barren.
Here, the mother is taken as the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*).
And "barren" (*vandhyā*) is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
When that [property] is being proven with respect to that very subject (*dharmin*), it is contradicted by "motherhood" (*mātṛtva*), which is established by one's own words.
As for this contradiction: by the word "mother," a woman characterized by the capacity to give birth is denoted; by the word "barren," the opposite of that is denoted.
And therefore, if she is a mother, how can she be barren?
And if she is barren, how can she be a mother?
Likewise, there is the "unestablished qualifier" (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*), as for example, when a Buddhist says to a Sāṃkhya, "Sound is perishable.
That which is not established is "unestablished."
That by which something is distinguished is a "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*), which is characterized as the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
Consequently, that in which the qualifier is unestablished is of such a kind. In this same manner, the interpretation of the words should be applied to the remaining cases as well.
And here, "sound" is the subject (nirdeśa);
"perishable" is the property to be proven (sādhyadharma).
Furthermore, this [reason] is one whose qualification is unestablished for the Buddhist with respect to the Sāṃkhya.
For in his established doctrine, nothing whatsoever is perishable.
As it has been said: "This triple world departs from its manifest state because of the negation of permanence;
yet even when departed, it exists because of the negation of destruction," and so forth [Yogasūtra 3.13].
[The Vyāsabhāṣya] says:
If this is so, then there is no such thing as a fallacious position (pakṣābhāsa).
For instance: the application of inference is for the sake of establishing a desired object when there is a disagreement;
and it is precisely this disagreement that causes the aforementioned fault—thus, why employ inference?
To this, it is replied:
It is not mere contradiction that constitutes the fault, because it is opposed by reasoning (*yukti*).
For instance, when proofs have been established through logical arguments and examples, the application of inference (*anumāna-prayoga*) occurs for the sake of establishing the intended object;
it does not occur otherwise.
Furthermore, because it depends upon proof,
one must first establish the example and then formulate the formal argument (*prayoga*);
however, if the example is not established, it is a fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*).
Thus, having made this digression.
Likewise, there is that which has an unestablished subject (*aprasiddhaviśeṣya*), such as for a Sāṃkhya saying to a Buddhist, "The self is conscious.
In this context, "subject" (*viśeṣya*) and "property-bearer" (*dharmin*) are synonymous;
and here, the self is the property-bearer.
The property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is "the state of being conscious" (cetanatva).
Thus, for the Sāṃkhya, this thesis (pakṣa) directed against the Buddhist has an unestablished subject (aprasiddhaviśeṣya),
because the self (ātman) is not established [for the Buddhist].
Because it is accepted that all phenomena are selfless,
the objection and its refutation are as before.
Likewise, there is the "unestablished for both" (aprasiddhobhaya), as for example,
when a Vaiśeṣika asserts to a Buddhist that the self (ātman) is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of pleasure and so forth;
in this case, both— the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin)— are unestablished.
In this context, the self (ātman) is the subject (dharmin).
Its being the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of pleasure and so forth is the property to be proven (sādhyadharma).
For according to the Vaiśeṣika, an effect arises from three types of causes.

Namely: from the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). For instance, the threads are the inherent cause of the cloth, the conjunction of the threads is the non-inherent cause, while the shuttle, loom, and so forth are the instrumental causes. In this same way, the self (*ātman*) is the inherent cause of pleasure, pain, desire, and the like.
The conjunction of the self and the mind is the non-inherent cause;
garlands, sandalwood, and so forth are the instrumental causes.
Thus, for the Vaiśeṣika, both [causes] are unestablished with respect to the Buddhist.
Its self (ātman) is neither established as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) nor is it the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*),
because it is admitted that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) alone possesses the power of production.
The objection and its refutation are as before.

"Having a well-known relationship" means that the relationship characterized by the property (dharma) and the subject (dharmin) is established between the proponent and the opponent through their lack of disagreement, as in the case of "sound is audible.
Here, sound is the subject, and audibility is the property to be proven.
Both of these are established for the proponent and the opponent.
Regarding the phrase "the statements of these" and so forth:
the word "of these" (eṣām) refers collectively to all nine [members].
The connection is that these are "faults of the proposition" (*pratijñādoṣa*). He states the reason:
by way of refuting the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the property (*dharma*), [the faults apply] to the first five.
"Self" (sva) and "that form" (tadrūpa) mean its own nature (svarūpa).
That by which something is refuted, or that which refutes, is "refutation" (nirākaraṇa);
it means negation (pratiṣedhana).
The negation of the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharmasvarūpa*) is the "face" (*mukha*); the sense is that it is like a face, meaning a door.

The negation of the intrinsic nature of phenomena itself is the face; thus, by way of the negation of the intrinsic nature of phenomena—that is, through the door of the refutation of the true reality of phenomena—the sound that is not audible is negated.

In these five [categories] beginning with "thus" (ityevamādi), the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) consists in the fact that the true nature of phenomena (*dharmayāthātmya*) is established through direct perception and the other means of valid cognition;
likewise, for the [remaining] three, it is because of the impossibility of such demonstration.
In this context, "demonstration" (*pratipādana*) refers to that by which something is demonstrated, or that which demonstrates.
The core meaning is "the supreme conviction.
Its impossibility is the impossibility of demonstration; therefore, it is due to the impossibility of demonstration.
Furthermore, demonstration is not possible when there is no comprehension of the example and so forth.
Likewise, because of the fruitlessness of the proof for a single [entity].
"Fruitlessness" (vaiphalya) is the state of being fruitless; the fruitlessness of the proof is "sādhanavaiphalya," and therefore it is "because of the fruitlessness of the proof.
The word "ca" (and) is used as a conjunction.
Furthermore, these are their statements:
"faults of the proposition" (*pratijñādoṣa*) and "the side of the proposition" (*pratijñāpakṣa*) are not different in meaning.
And the term "fallacy of a fault" (doṣābhāsa) is likewise applicable.
Thus have the fallacies of the thesis (pakṣābhāsa) been explained.
Now, wishing to state the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), he says:
"The unestablished (*asiddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and the contradictory (*viruddha*) are the fallacious reasons.
Thus, the unestablished, the inconclusive, and the contradictory are [collectively] called "the unestablished, inconclusive, and contradictory."

They are called "pseudo-reasons" (*hetvābhāsa*) because they appear to be reasons. Adhering to the principle that "the explanation follows the enumeration," he speaks with the desire to explain the unestablished (*asiddha*). Among these, the unestablished is of four kinds.
In this context, regarding these [fallacies] such as the unestablished (*asiddha*):
that which is established is "established" (*siddha*), meaning it is recognized; that which is not established is "unestablished" (*asiddha*), meaning it is not recognized.
It is of four kinds, having four divisions.
He shows the various types, as follows:
"unestablished for both," and so forth.
"Namely" (*tadyathā*) is as before.
That which is unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent is "unestablished for both" (*ubhayāsiddha*).
That which is unestablished for either the proponent or the opponent is called "unestablished for one of the two" (anyatarāsiddha).
That which is doubted is "doubtful"; because it is doubtful, it is unestablished; thus, it is called "unestablished due to doubt" (*saṃdigdhasiddha*).
The substratum is the locus; that [reason] for which this is unestablished is "unestablished in its substratum" (āśrayāsiddha).
The word "and" (ca) has the sense of conjunction.
The word "iti" indicates the conclusion.
Now he states the examples,
beginning with "In that regard, concerning the impermanence of sound," and so forth.
The word "therein" (tatra) is as explained previously.

When the non-eternality of sound is to be proven, in the argument "sound is non-eternal because it is visible" (*cākṣuṣatvāt*), "visible" means that which is graspable by the sense organ of sight; the state of being so is "visibility. Therefore, this reason is unestablished for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*).
For instance, visibility is established neither for the proponent nor for the opponent,
because sound is apprehended by the sense organ of hearing.
"Because it is produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*) is unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*) against one who maintains that sound is manifested.
This is said with respect to the probandum "sound is eternal.
Thus, this reason, "because it is produced," is unestablished for one of the two parties—namely, against the Mīmāṃsaka or the Kāpila—who maintain that sound is manifested.
For instance, sound is not produced by his palate, lips, and so forth; rather, it is manifested.

"Likewise, by way of being vapor and so forth," and so on. Vapor (*bāṣpa*) originates from water and the like; it is the "beginning" (*ādi*) of that which includes dust, smoke, and so forth—this is "vapor and the rest" (*bāṣpādi*). Its "state" (*bhāva*) is its existence (*sattā*); [the term] "by way of being vapor and so forth" means by means of that state. "Being doubted" (*saṃdihyamānaḥ*) means falling into doubt, as in: "Is this smoke, or is it vapor, or is it dust or smoke? (*reṇuvarti*).

The "aggregate of elements" (bhūtasaṃghāta) is a subtle collection of earth and the other [elements]. What [is it for]? It is for the accomplishment of fire (agnisiddhi); that is, in that accomplishment of fire.
When it is taught or stated that "there is fire here because of smoke," this is a "doubtful-unestablished" (saṃdigdhāsiddha) reason;
for only smoke that is ascertained as such leads to the cognition of fire, not smoke that is unascertained.
The same applies to such cases as "space is a substance."
"Space" is the indication of the subject (*dharmin*);
"substance" is the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*);
and its qualities are six.
Namely: number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, and sound.

In this context, "the state of being a substratum of qualities" means that which is the substratum of qualities; its reality is its essence. Therefore, [the reason] is "because of being a substratum of qualities. This reason is *āśrayāsiddha* (unestablished in its locus) with respect to the Buddhist who maintains the non-existence of space (*ākāśa*), because the subject itself is unestablished.
And thus is his established doctrine:
"O monks, these five are mere designations, mere conventionalities, mere propositions, mere worldly conventions, and mere conceptual constructions. Which five?"
The past time, the future time, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), space, and the person (*pudgala*). But is there not also another [type of] unestablished reason? And that is twofold:
the unestablished because it is a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśāsiddha*).
For example: "Sound is impermanent because it is impermanent," which is unestablished due to lack of pervasion;
and "Trees are sentient because they sleep."
"Why was it not mentioned? The Teacher replied,
"Because it is included [within another category]."
If it is asked, "Where, then, is its inclusion? [the answer is] that since both [the subject and the reason] are unestablished, there is no fault. He says:
If this is so, let there be only two types of unestablished [reasons], namely the unestablished for both parties (ubhayāsiddha) and the unestablished for one of the two parties (anyatarāsiddha),
since the remaining two are included within these very categories.
And thus it has been said by others as well:
The two types of unestablished [reasons] belong either to both [parties] or to one of the two.
And so forth. This is not so;
for a specific distinction is established by means of the subject (*dharmin*), the reason (*hetu*), and the condition (*upādhi*) which gives rise to doubt.
Furthermore, the composition of this treatise has as its fruit the instruction of those to be trained (*vineya*).
Enough has been said regarding the unestablished [reason] in detail.
Now, the inconclusive (anaikāntika) is being discussed;
it is of six kinds, that is, sixfold. That which exists exclusively is "exclusive" (aikāntika).
"Not one-sided" means not exclusively certain;
"of six kinds" means having six modes, that is to say, sixfold.
He states the divisions themselves,
beginning with "common" (*sādhāraṇa*), and so forth;
[these names] are literal.
We shall provide an example of this very point:
therein, [the reason] "because of being knowable" is common [to both sides], such that [the subject] is eternal.
Here, the word "therein" (tatra) is as explained previously.

That which is common to two or many is "shared" (*sādhāraṇa*). "Knowable" (*prameya*) means that which is measured (*pramīyate*), that is to say, that which is to be known; its state is "knowability" (*prameyatva*). Therefore, from "knowability," meaning from being delimited by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
in the phrase "it is eternal," the subject (*dharmin*) designated as "sound" is understood.
And this [reason] is a cause for doubt because it is common to both similar instances (sapakṣa) and their opposites, such as space and a jar;
as it has been said:
"For that [reason], whether it be eternal or non-eternal," and so forth.
That state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) is the property (*dharma*).
Indeed, in order to demonstrate its form:
"eternal" (*nitya*) and "non-eternal" (*anitya*) are [the two]; both eternal and non-eternal are "eternal-and-non-eternal"; and those two are the two sides, thus "eternal-and-non-eternal-sides."
The meaning is: "of those two positions, namely the eternal and the non-eternal.
What [is the consequence]?
Because it is common—that is, because it functions equally with respect to both—it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
The [author] demonstrates this very application:

"Is sound impermanent because it is an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), like a jar; or rather, is it permanent because it is an object of knowledge, like space? This is shown for the sake of clarity.
[The opponent replies: "Ah! This is not a cause for doubt."

Because doubt exists even prior to this application [of the reason], it is impossible for the presence of the reason to be invariably concomitant with the presence of that [doubt]. And it has been said:
"The various types of inconclusive reasons (*anaikāntika*) are not at all causes of doubt."
When there is doubt and a reason has been stated, because the existence [of that reason] is not restricted [to the subject alone].
And so forth. This is not so; for doubt is not intended [as a necessary condition], and because the formulation of the argument is possible even without it.
Furthermore, a formal argument (prayoga) is also employed for the purpose of refuting those whose minds are perverted;
even in that case, it is called "inconclusive" (anaikāntika) because it serves as a cause for doubt.
"Because of audibility, [sound] is eternal; this is the uncommon [reason]," and so forth.

"Uncommon" means distinct from the common; that is, it is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) that, being non-common, is excluded from both the similar instances (sapakṣa) and the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).
He provides an example:
"Because it is audible, it is eternal.

"Audible" (*śrāvaṇa*) means that which is graspable by the faculty of hearing; the state of being so is "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*). From that [audibility], it follows that it is "eternal," meaning indestructible.
It is understood that "sound" [is the subject].

In this regard, this property of audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*), having abandoned its own locus (the subject), exists neither in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) such as space (*ākāśa*), nor in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) such as a jar (*ghaṭa*); thus, it is a cause for doubt.
For this very reason, he says:
"Regarding 'tad dhi' and so forth:
*tat* refers to that property of being audible (*śrāvaṇatva*).
The word *hi* is used for the purpose of illustration; [it is so called] because it is excluded from both the categories of the eternal and the non-eternal."
The connection is that [the reason] is a cause for doubt.
Furthermore, in order to refute the claim that "it will exist elsewhere," he says:
"Because nothing else exists that is either distinct from the eternal or the non-eternal."
Whatever exists must be either permanent or impermanent, and not otherwise,
because of contradiction and the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, it is a cause of doubt, meaning a ground for uncertainty.
He asks "How so?
and says "Of what kind," and so forth;
that is, of what nature is this—whether it be permanent or, on the other hand, impermanent?
What is meant is that the sound under discussion possesses audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*).
If that [audibility] were perceived elsewhere—whether in something eternal or non-eternal—then, by virtue of that fact, a determination regarding the other case would be appropriate;
otherwise it would not, because even the postulation of a contrary possibility would have its scope restricted by the presence of another instance.
Much could be said on this point; enough of this digression.
The objections and their refutations are as before.
In this manner, it should also be cultivated for the remaining [elements].
"Residing in a portion of the similar class," and so forth.

A similar class (*sapakṣa*) is that which is similar to the subject (*pakṣa*); a portion of that is "a portion of the similar class" (*sapakṣaikadeśa*). That which resides in this [portion] is "residing in a portion of the similar class" (*sapakṣaikadeśavṛtti*).
Likewise, a dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is that which is unlike the subject; that which has the nature of pervading that is "pervading the dissimilar class" (*vipakṣavyāpī*).
He states an example: for instance,
"Sound is not produced immediately after an effort, because it is eternal."
Sound is the subject (dharmin).
The property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is the state of not being immediately subsequent to effort.
"Because of impermanence" is the logical reason (hetu).
In this context, the subject (*pakṣa*) is "that which does not follow immediately upon human effort" (*aprayatnānantarīyaka*).
The object (*artha*) is "that which does not follow immediately upon human effort.
What is the collection of entities (*padārthasaṃghāta*) to be proven (*sādhya*) for this [subject]? It is lightning, space, and so forth.
The similar instance (sapakṣa) is that; the property of impermanence exists in one part of it, such as lightning and so forth, but not in [other parts] such as space,
because the latter is eternal.
Likewise, for this [reason], the subject (*pakṣa*) is that which does not follow immediately after effort, while its counter-subject (*vipakṣa*) is things such as a jar;
in all such cases, including jars and the like, impermanence exists,
because that which follows immediately after effort is impermanent.

Since this is so, therefore this impermanence as well—by way of its similarity to a flash of lightning, that is, by being equal to a flash of lightning—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). He states the objection regarding the nature of things: "Is it, like a jar, immediately following from effort because of its impermanence?"
Is sound, like lightning and so forth, non-eternal because it is not produced immediately after an effort?
[This is] for the sake of clarity.
The [reason] that exists in a portion of the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) while pervading the similar instances (sapakṣa) is easily understood through its compound form. He states an example:
For example: "Sound is produced immediately after effort because it is impermanent.
Here, "produced immediately after effort" is the subject (pakṣa), while "the jar and so forth" is its similar instance (sapakṣa).
Impermanence exists in all such cases, such as the jar and so forth.
The subject (*pakṣa*) is that which follows immediately after effort; its counter-subject (*vipakṣa*) consists of lightning, space, and so forth.
Among these, impermanence exists in one part, such as lightning, but not in [others], such as space.
Therefore, this [reason] is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) as before, by virtue of its similarity to a jar struck by lightning; such is the meaning of the Sūtra.
It should be contemplated through one's own intelligence by means of the opposite of what has been stated.
"Occurring in one part of both sides":
that which occurs in one part of both sides—namely, the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)—is "that which occurs in one part of both sides.
He provides an example:
For example: "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal."
The eternal category—such as space, atoms, and so forth—is its similar instance (*sapakṣa*).
Within that, the property of incorporeality exists in part, such as in space, but not in atoms and the like.
The non-eternal category—such as a pot, pleasure, and so forth—is its dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
In that regard, incorporeality exists in one part [of the subject], such as pleasure and so forth, but not in jars and the like.
Therefore, this too is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by virtue of the common property between pleasure and space.
This sūtra is also established by its literal meaning.
Likewise, there is the *viruddhāvyabhicārī* (the non-erroneous contradictory).
A *viruddha* (contradictory) reason is one that establishes a meaning contrary to the subject matter of the reason under consideration.
A *viruddhāvyabhicārī* is so called because it does not deviate from what is contradictory (*viruddham na vyabhicarati*).

The meaning is that, having been presented, it does not deviate from its counter-positive (pratiyogin) because it does not exclude such a thing as its object. Therefore, he says this: "Having set aside the probandum by means of this [reason], the application of the logical reason (hetu) must be made.
Others, however, explain it as "the non-deviating contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*), meaning that which is both contradictory and non-deviating.
This, however, is indeed untenable,
because it is contradictory and results in the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anekānta).
He provides an example:
For example: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot," and "Sound is permanent because it is audible, like the nature of sound.
Since both are causes for doubt, these two together constitute a single inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*).
When the Vaiśeṣika has stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar," the Mīmāṃsaka says:
"Sound is permanent because it is audible, like the nature of sound (*śabdatva*).

For that which is called the 'nature of sound'—the basis for the uniform designation and cognition 'sound' across all sounds differentiated by distinctions such as flute, lute, drum, and tabor—is a specific universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) and is permanent."
"Because both are causes of doubt.
This means that within a single subject (*dharmin*), both—namely, being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and being audible (*śrāvaṇatva*)—are causes of doubt, that is, causes of uncertainty.

Thus, in a single subject, the two reasons called "being produced" and "being audible" produce doubt: "Is it impermanent because of being produced, like a jar? Or is it permanent because of being audible, like soundness (*śabdatva*)?"
When it has been established in this way that [the two reasons] are causes of doubt, the opponent objects: "Are they causes of doubt when combined, or when separate?
If they are causes of doubt when combined, then they do not differ from the 'uncommon' (asādhāraṇa) reason; and audibility (śrāvaṇatva) has been stated to be of the nature of the uncommon."
Nor does it [arise] from the two taken separately,
because the two taken separately lack the nature of a correct cause.
To this, it is said:
Both [types] together alone constitute the cause of doubt.
Now, it was argued that this does not differ from the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) reason;
but that is not so.
Because it is indeed distinct from [the other two types],
namely the "incompatible non-deviant" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) which is mutually dependent;
whereas this one is "single," meaning it is without a companion and uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*).
And since this [reason] has been distinguished and adopted by the Teacher in this particular aspect, there is no fault.
Furthermore, it is stated in the root text: "Both of these are non-conclusive (anaikāntika) only when combined;
however, when they are not manifested, that [non-conclusiveness] is absent."
Much could be said on this matter, but it is not stated here;
this undertaking is for the sake of favoring those beings who prefer conciseness.
Thus, what was stated is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Now he explains the contradictory [reason]: "The contradictory is of four kinds," and so forth.

It is called "contradictory" because it is contradicted; for indeed, this [reason] is necessarily contradicted by either a property (*dharma*) or a subject (*dharmin*) that establishes the opposite of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and other attributes of the property. Thus, it is of four kinds, meaning it has four divisions.
For example:
"proving that which is contrary to the true nature of phenomena," and so forth.
The phrase "for example" (*tadyathā*) is intended to introduce specific instances.
We shall explain the meaning of the term "example" (*udāharaṇa*) in the section on examples itself.
Regarding that, [the phrase] "in that case, dharma... and so forth:
therein, an example that establishes the opposite of the nature of the property (*dharma*) is as follows: "it is eternal," as previously stated.

"Dharma" and "paryāya" are synonymous. Its "intrinsic nature" (svarūpa) is its unique characteristic (asādhāraṇa-ātmalakṣaṇa), which constitutes the essence of dharma; thus, the compound [viparīta-sādhana] means "that which proves the opposite of that.
This should be understood in the same way for the remaining cases as well.
Now he states an example:

"For instance, [in the argument] 'Sound is eternal because it is produced, or because it follows immediately upon effort,' this reason is contradictory by its presence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) alone.
Here, the nature of the property (*dharma*) is eternity."
And this [reason] establishes impermanence, which is the opposite of the reason [adduced by the opponent], because it is invariably concomitant with that very [impermanence]. Thus he said:
The contradictory [reason] is so called because it exists only in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
An objection is raised: "Since this does not exist in the subject (*pakṣadharma*), it is no different from the unestablished (*asiddha*); how then can it be called contradictory?
To this, it is replied:

Contradiction is not necessarily restricted to that which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) alone, for the Teacher’s activity proceeds otherwise as well; this is because he intends to indicate the application [of the definition] to what is under discussion. Furthermore, this [type of contradiction] is not indistinguishable from the unestablished (*asiddha*).
Because it is unestablished as proving the opposite,
and because the presentation [of the argument] has this as its primary purpose;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) would be unestablished.
Since even properties such as "knowability" (prameyatva) are unestablished when used as proofs for [qualities] like eternality,
enough with this digression; this is merely a sketch of the argument.

An example of "proving the opposite of a specific property" (*dharmaviśeṣaviparītasādhana*) is as follows: "The eyes and so forth exist for the sake of another, because they are composite, like the parts of a bed or a seat.
Who, then, says this? A Sāṃkhya speaking to a Buddhist.
In this context, the subjects (*dharmin*) are the eye and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the remaining sense organs, the Great Principle (*mahat*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and so on.
The property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*).
And its specific qualification is intended to be "being for the sake of another who is not a composite";
otherwise, there would be the consequence of a deficiency in the formal argument due to the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
The reason (*hetu*) is "because of being a composite" (*saṃghātatvāt*).
In this context, the meeting of two or many is a "conglomeration" (*saṃghāta*); its state is "conglomerateness" (*saṃghātatva*). [The argument is: "Because of that conglomerateness.
The example is "like the parts of a bed, a seat, and so forth.
A "bed" (*śayana*) refers to a couch (*palyaṅka*) and the like.
A seat refers to a chair and so forth;
its constituent parts are indeed well known.
The intended meaning is that just as these parts exist for the sake of another—such as Devadatta—because they are an aggregate, so too do the eye and the other sense faculties.

Now he states the contradiction, beginning with "this" (ayam): this reason, characterized by being a composite (saṃghātatva), just as it establishes the state of being for the sake of another (pārārthya)— that is, the quality of serving another's purpose— of the eyes and so forth, in that very same manner, it [also] establishes their own state of being a composite.
It also establishes that the supreme self possesses parts,
because [the property in question] is invariably concomitant with that as well.
And so it has been said:
"Because of non-deviation in both cases.
"In both cases" means because [the reason] is non-deviant—that is, indicative—in both the case of being for another's sake (*parārtha*) and in the case of being a composite (*saṃhatatva*).
And thus, it can indeed be stated in this way as well: "The eyes and so forth are for another's sake and are composites, because they are composites, like the parts of a bed or a seat."
For the parts such as the bed and the seat perform their function only for that which is a composite whole possessing hands, feet, thighs, neck, and so forth, and not for anything else;
thus it is "because of perception.
[The opponent] says: Since it exists only in the counter-example (vipakṣa), it is contradictory (viruddha); this is the general definition of a contradictory reason. How, then, is it applicable here?
It is said:
for it is observed that the term "composite" (*saṃhata*) occurs in reference to that very thing which is the opposite of the non-composite (*asaṃhata*);
what, then, is not tenable?
The objection and its refutation are as before.
"Contrary to the nature of the subject (dharmin)," and so forth.
A "subject" (dharmin) is that which possesses properties (dharmas);
an example is, for instance, "it is not a substance," and so on.
Who, then, speaks thus? A Vaiśeṣika speaking to the Buddhists. By what connection, however, [is this said]? Thus [he asks].
It is said:
its established doctrine is that there are six categories (padārtha): substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence.
From among these, the substances are earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind.
There are twenty-four qualities (*guṇa*).
