Those stated in the Sūtra are: color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort.
By the word "and" (*ca*), fluidity, heaviness, mental impression (*saṃskāra*), viscidity, merit and demerit (*dharmādharmau*), and sound are included.
Thus, there are twenty-four qualities and five actions.
These actions are as follows: throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and locomotion.
By the mention of "going," activities such as wandering, moving upward, shaking, and pulsating are included.

Generality (*sāmānya*) is of two kinds: the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). Among these, the higher is existence (*sattā*), being (*bhāva*), and is called the "great generality" (*mahāsāmānya*).
Furthermore, there are categories such as substantiality (dravyatva) and so forth.
Among these, existence (sattā) is an entity distinct from substance, quality, and action. By what reasoning is this so? To this, he says:
"Being an entity is not a substance because it possesses a single substance" is the reason (*hetu*).
"Like generality and particularity" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Now, the meaning of the term "entity" (*bhāva*) is stated.
"Substance is not an entity";
the meaning is that it is other than substance.

Regarding the phrase "because of possessing a single substance": that which is both one and a substance is a "single substance" (*ekadravya*); since this [quality] has such a thing as its substrate (*āśraya*), it is "possessing a single substance" (*ekadravyavān*).
Because of the statement that "a *bahuvrīhi* compound with terms in apposition is sometimes a *karmadhāraya*, as in the case of 'possessing all wealth' (*sarvadhana*) and so forth";
"that state" means "reality" (*tattva*), and therefore, "because of having a single substance" means because of existing in a single substance.
For the Vaiśeṣika, substance is of two kinds: non-substantial substance and multi-substantial substance.
Among these, non-substantial substances are space, time, direction, self, and atoms;
whereas multi-substantial substances are aggregates beginning with dyads (dvyaṇuka).
But a single substance does not exist as a substance at all;
rather, an entity (bhāva) possesses a single substance.
Therefore, because it is characterized differently from the definition of a substance, an entity is not a substance.
The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is a commonality-cum-particularity (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*),
and it is characterized by substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*).
For substantiality is a commonality because it exists in the nine substances, and it is a particularity because it distinguishes [substances] from qualities and actions.
In this same way, the conceptualization (*bhāvanā*) of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) and "action-ness" (*karmatva*) must also be performed.

Consequently, that which is both a universal (*sāmānya*) and a particular (*viśeṣa*) is a "universal-particular" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*); it exists as something similar to that, and thus it is "possessing a universal-particular" (*sāmānyaviśeṣavat*).
The meaning is: like "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*).
And from this, the following is implied:

just as among the nine substances, that which exists in each individual one is not "substance" (dravya) itself, but rather the universal-particular characteristic known as "substanceness" (dravyatva), so too is the case with "being" (bhāva); such is the intended meaning. He says this, wishing to refute the claim: "Even if it is not a substance, it will nonetheless be a quality (guṇa) or an action (karman). He states: [the following].
And because [the term "existence"] applies to qualities and actions, existence is not a quality; for it applies to qualities, just as "quality-ness" (guṇatva) does.
Furthermore, if existence were a quality, it would not subsist in qualities, because qualities are themselves devoid of qualities.
And existence resides in qualities,
because there is the cognition "the quality exists.
Likewise, action is not existence, because existence resides in actions, just as [resides] in the state of being an action (*karmatva*).
Furthermore, if being (*bhāva*) were itself an action, then it would not reside within actions, because actions are devoid of further action;
yet being does reside within actions,
as is evident from the cognition "a good action."
The presentation of the reversal [of the order] is for the purpose of demonstrating various logical methods regarding the thesis and the reason.
When the Vaiśeṣika has spoken thus, the Buddhist says:
"And this reason, though of three kinds, just as it establishes the negation of substance and so forth, likewise establishes the non-existence of the subject (dharmin) which is an entity."
Because it is also invariably concomitant with that;
and so it has been said:
"Because there is no deviation in either case."
Because it serves as a means of cognition for both the negation of substance and so forth, and for existence and non-existence;

and thus, just as it can be said that "existence is not a substance because it consists of a single substance, like substanceness," so too can this be said: "existence is not indeed existence because it consists of a single substance, like substanceness."
Furthermore, substantiality (*dravyatva*) is not an entity (*bhāva*), because it is a generality-particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).
Likewise, [substance] is not a quality (*guṇa*), because it exists in qualities, just as the nature of quality (*guṇatva*) does.
Here too, an entity is not itself an entity, because it exists in qualities, just as the nature of quality does.
Furthermore, quality-ness (*guṇatva*) is not an entity (*bhāva*), precisely because it is a particular universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*).

Likewise, action (*karman*) is not an entity, because it exists within actions, just as action-ness (*karmatva*) does; here too, being-ness (*bhāvatva*) is not an entity, because it exists within actions, just as action-ness does.
Nor is action-ness an entity, because it is a particular universal.
However, applying the definition of the "contradictory to the universal" (*sāmānyaviruddha*) is indeed easy, because the particular (*viśeṣa*) is the opposite of the universal (*bhāva*).
[The opponent] says: "This [reason] does not differ from the unestablished (*asiddha*); how then can it be contradictory? For instance:
For the Buddhists, there is no such thing as "existence" (bhāva) that exists as something distinct from substance and so forth;
and because of its non-existence, the reason is indeed unestablished in its locus (āśrayāsiddha).
To this it is replied: this is true.
However, even that which is established for the opponent is called "contradictory" (*viruddha*) if it pervades only the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), because this is for the sake of illustration.
Furthermore, since multiple types of fallacies may occur even in a single case, there is no fault here, as it is intended to demonstrate those specific distinctions.
He says: "In this way, there is no state of non-contradiction anywhere, because of the presence of contradictions regarding specific [qualities]. No.
Since the opposing [objection] is removed by the very force of the corroborative example (dṛṣṭānta) associated with the authorized reason (hetu),

even so, when there is an objection based on a contradiction— such as "Sound is impermanent because it is cookable, like a pot," or "Sound is cookable"— that [objection] is removed by the power of another example, such as a cloth, which is associated with the reason of being produced (kṛtakatva) and is not cookable; for it is indeed admitted that [the original reason] remains unrefuted when the contradiction is thus removed.
Furthermore, its exclusion from this [category] is impossible, because the property of residing in a single substance does not occur elsewhere apart from it.
Much could be said on this point; enough of this digression.
An example of a reason that proves the opposite of a specific property of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviparītasādhana*) is as follows:
the subject is existence itself, and its specific property is "being the agent of the notion of 'existent'.
For it has been said: "That because of which [the notions] 'existent' occur with respect to substances, qualities, and actions—that is *sattā* (existence)."
An example of a reason that proves the opposite [of what is intended] is as follows:

this very same reason called "possessing a single substance," within this very same prima facie argument characterized by the thesis "existence is not a substance" and so forth, proves the opposite of that specific property of the subject called "existence"— namely, its being the producer of the cognition of "existent"— which is the state of being the producer of the cognition of "non-existent."
Because that too is pervaded [by the same reason].
For it can indeed be stated as follows: "Existence (bhāva) is not the producer of the cognition 'existent' (sat-pratyaya), because it possesses a single substance, like substanceness (dravyatva).
And substanceness is not the producer of the cognition 'existent', because it is the producer of the cognition of a substance."
The same should be stated regarding the cause as a quality (*guṇa*), an action (*karman*), or an entity (*bhāva*).
Therefore it was said: "because of non-deviation in both cases," which has the meaning already explained.
The objection and its refutation are as before.
The fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) have been explained.
Now is the occasion for the fallacies of the example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*);
they are now being stated.
In that regard, just as the example is twofold, so too is its semblance (*tadābhāsa*) with respect to the distinction of its fundamental types.
He said:
"The semblance of an example is twofold."
By way of similarity and by way of dissimilarity,
the example (dṛṣṭānta) has the definition already stated.
That which appears like an example but is not one is a pseudo-example (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa).

The meaning is "resembling an example. In that regard, first, the fallacious example by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) is of five kinds, having five divisions, as follows: "unestablished in the property of the probans" (*sādhanadharmāsiddha*), and so forth.

The phrase "tadyathā" (for example) is for the purpose of illustrating the various types [of fallacies]. A probative property (*sādhanadharma*) that is unestablished (*asiddha*) is called "non-existent.
Consequently, when a probative property is unestablished in this [subject], it is termed "the unestablished probative property" (*sādhanadharmāsiddha*).

However, it is not the case that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound a word ending in a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) must necessarily precede; thus, [the term] "asiddhasādhanadharmāḥ" is not unestablished.

Nor is there a problem regarding compounds such as *ahitāgni*, because such words belong to the class of *āhitāgni* and so forth, which is an open-ended group (*ākṛtigaṇa*) where the order is optional.
Others, however, explain that it is "unestablished due to the unestablishment of the probans" (sādhanadharmāsiddha) because it is devoid of the property that serves as the probans;
yet this is not at all elegant.
The same should be understood for the cases of the unestablishment of the property to be proven (sādhya) and the unestablishment of both properties.
We shall explain the meaning of terms such as "positive concomitance" (anvaya) in the section on examples;
since that occasion has now arrived, they are being pointed out in their proper order.
Among these, an example of the unestablished property of the probans (sādhanadharma-asiddha) is as follows:
"Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal. The word "yathā" (just as) is used for the purpose of introducing an example.
"Sound is eternal" is the proposition (*pratijñā*), which constitutes the subject (*pakṣa*).
"Because of being formless" is the reason (*hetu*).

He states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*): "Whatever entity is formless is observed to be eternal, such as an atom (*paramāṇu*). This constitutes the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Since it is precisely these [cognitions] appearing as such that are under discussion,
no example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) has been presented;
furthermore, this [example] is intended to be one that conforms to both the property to be proven (sādhya) and the probans (sādhana).
But here, the property to be proven exists, whereas the proving property does not;
and thus it has been said:
for in the case of an atom, the property to be proven—eternality—exists.
Because it is eternal by virtue of being the ultimate cause,
the probans-property of "formlessness" does not exist [in it].
Why?
Because atoms possess corporeality;
and corporeality is established by the perception of corporeal effects such as jars and the like.
An example of one where the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is unestablished is as follows:
"Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like cognition.
[The argument is: whatever entity is incorporeal is seen to be eternal, as is the case with cognition.

For in the case of cognition (*buddhi*), the property of the means of proof (*sādhanadharma*)—immateriality (*amūrtatva*)—exists, whereas the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—eternality (*nityatva*)—does not exist, because cognition is non-eternal. Thus, the formulation of the syllogism (*sūtraprayoga*) is indeed easy to understand.
He demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*):
whatever thing is immaterial is seen to be eternal, as is the case with cognition.
He asks: "How is this [reason] unestablished with respect to the property to be proven (sādhyadharma)? To this, he replies:
"For in the intellect (buddhi), the property of proof (sādhanadharma), namely incorporeality (amūrtatva), exists."
Because its formlessness is perceived,
the property to be proven— eternality— is absent.
Why?
Because cognition is impermanent.
The unestablished for both [parties] is of two kinds. How so? To this he says: "existent and non-existent."
"Existing" (*sann*) refers to that which is non-established for both [parties] because it exists;
and "non-existing" (*asann*) refers to that which is non-established for both because it does not exist.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) should be understood as the fundamental one itself.
As it has been said:
"In that case, [the example] 'like a jar' is unestablished for both parties because it does not exist [for them].

Consequently, in the argument "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like a jar," neither the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), characterized by eternality, nor the proving property (*sādhanadharma*), characterized by incorporeality, exists in the jar; for a jar is impermanent and corporeal.
Likewise, [the reason] "like space" (*ākāśavat*) is unestablished for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*).

Therefore, regarding the argument "sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like space," one might object: "Since both terms are established, how can it be unestablished for both? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Against one who asserts its non-existence" means against the Buddhist who asserts the non-existence of space;
that is to say, against the Sāṃkhya.
For when that [self] exists, there is reflection on attributes such as permanence, and not otherwise.
"Ananvaya," and so forth: "ananvaya" means that the concomitance (*anvaya*) is non-existent; the meaning is that the concomitance has not been demonstrated.
*Anvaya*, *anugama*, and *vyāpti* are synonymous.
He states its definition with the words "where," and so forth.

He states the subject matter with the word "where": "without anvaya" means without the observation of pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans—that is, between the thing to be established and the reason. "Coexistence" (*sahabhāva*) is merely their presence in a single locus.
It is demonstrated, stated, and explained;
it is not by way of repetition that the reason is established among those things that follow from what is to be proven.
He states an example:
Just as in the case of a jar, where being produced and impermanence are observed,
the jar is thus the substratum (āśraya) of both being produced and impermanence;

yet, since this merely states a relationship of substratum and dependent (āśrayāśrayibhāva), and because deviation (vyabhicāra) is possible elsewhere, it is impossible for this to establish the intended object.
"Contrary positive concomitance" (*viparītānvaya*) and so forth:
that in which the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), meaning the following or agreement (*anugama*), is "contrary," that is, functions in a reversed manner, is of such a kind. He provides an example.
When one should say, "Whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent," he says instead, "Whatever is impermanent is seen to be produced.
Thus, without first uttering the property of the reason (*sādhanadharma*), he utters the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
He says:
If one asks, "Even so, what is the fault? it is replied:
"It is a transgression of the seal of logic."
This is because there is an exception to the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

For instance, in the argument "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort," if one were to say "whatever is impermanent, that follows immediately upon effort," this would be fallacious;
for although lightning and other such things are impermanent, they do not follow immediately upon effort.
Thus, enough of this digression;
this concludes the fallacious examples of the similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).
Also by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*);
not only by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) alone. What [is it]?
The fallacious example (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa) has its meaning previously determined;
it is of five kinds.
It is as follows: "not excluded from the probandum" (*sādhyāvyāvṛtta*), and so forth.

In this context, "probandum" (*sādhya*) means that which is recognized [as the property to be proven]; "not excluded from that" means not excluded from the probandum, hence "not excluded from the probandum.
The objection and its refutation are as before.
The same should be stated regarding [the fallacies] where the reason is not excluded from both the similar and dissimilar instances.
However, we shall explain the meaning of terms such as "non-exclusion" (*avyatireka*) specifically in the section on the example (*udāharaṇa*),
for that is precisely the occasion that has now arrived.
Among these, [the reason] that does not exclude the probandum (*sādhyāvyāvṛtta*) is as follows: "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like an atom.
The word "like" (*yathā*) is for the purpose of introducing an example.
"Sound is eternal" is the proposition (*pratijñā*).

"Because of being formless" is the reason (*hetu*). Since the fallacious example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) is the subject under discussion, the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) has not been stated; however, space (*ākāśa*) and so forth should be inferred [as such].

The example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*), however, is the atom (*paramāṇu*); and this is correctly accepted as being devoid of the properties of the probandum, the probans, and both. For it has been said:

"It is stated that the non-existence of the reason [is established] precisely when there is an absence of the probandum," and so forth; and he says, "But this is not so," because [it would follow] from the perspective of the atom.
The probans (hetu) is the property that serves as the means of proof.
He demonstrates this very point by saying "immateriality" (amūrtatvam);
"excluded" (vyāvṛtta) means ceased or withdrawn.
Why?
Because atoms possess corporeality (*mūrtatva*).
The property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is permanence (*nityatva*), and that [corporeality] is not excluded from it.
Why?
Because atoms are eternal.
He said:

Among the fallacies of the similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), the one where the property of the means of proof (*sādhana-dharma*) is unestablished was stated first; why, then, is it stated here as "not excluded from the probandum" (*sādhya-avyāvṛtta*)?

Because that [previous case] has positive concomitance (*anvaya*) as its primary feature, and because positive concomitance consists in the formulation of the property of the probandum following the property of the means of proof.
Negation (vyatireka), however, consists in the exclusion of both: namely, the absence of the reason where there is an absence of the probandum.
Therefore, it is not excluded from the probandum.
Likewise, [the reason] is not excluded from the locus of the probandum (*sādhanāvyāvṛtta*), as in the case of action (*karman*).
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is exactly as before;
however, the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is action.
And that [quality] includes throwing upward and so forth. In that case, the property of permanence to be established for action is excluded,
because action is impermanent.
The probans is the property that serves as the means of proof;
he demonstrates that very thing by saying "immateriality.
That [property] is not excluded [from the subject].
Because action is formless.
"Excluded from both [categories] like space"—
this is the formal argument (prayoga) establishing permanence, which, as before, is provided with examples based on similarity such as atoms and so forth;
however, the example based on dissimilarity is "space."
For [the property of being] from space is neither excluded from permanence nor from incorporeality.
Why?
Because space is eternal and formless.
"Non-exclusion," and so forth.
"Non-exclusion" (avyatireka) means that exclusion (vyatireka) is non-existent; the meaning is that the exclusion has not been demonstrated.
He states its definition:
"Where the state of being a counter-example [to the pervasion] is demonstrated without the exclusion of the probandum and the probans"—this is what he means by "where. He explains it as:

"without the exclusion of the probandum and the probans" in the context of the present formal argument, characterized by such statements as, "whatever is impermanent is seen to be corporeal," and so forth.
The state of being its opposite (tadvipakṣabhāva) refers merely to the state of being the opposite of both the probandum and the probans;
that is to say, it is shown or demonstrated.
He states an example:
Just as impermanence and corporeality are observed in a jar,

so too, by stating merely the subject in one instance and not explicitly demonstrating the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), it is understood through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) that the [reason] establishes the intended object, because of the excessive burden of [unnecessary] exposition.
"Contrary negative concomitance" (*viparītavyatireka*), and so forth.
That in which the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—defined as previously stated—is "contrary," that is to say, inverted, is of such a kind.
He demonstrates that very point:
Regarding the passage beginning with "that which is impermanent" and so forth:

while in the very context of the formal argument (*prayoga*) provided with a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), one ought to teach the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) by stating, "Whatever is impermanent is seen to be corporeal"; yet instead, he says, "Whatever is corporeal is seen to be impermanent."
He asked: "Even so, what is the fault? It is replied:

There is deviation (vyabhicāra) elsewhere; for instance, in the case [of the argument] "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately after effort," the negative concomitance (vyatireka)— namely, "whatever does not follow immediately after effort is permanent"—
is deviant with respect to lightning.
Concluding [the discussion], he says:
"Of these," and so forth.
This refers to the statements of the fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*), reason (*hetvābhāsa*), and example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) of the forms previously described.
Why is it not a valid means of proof?
Precisely because it is a fallacy.
What then?
This is called a semblance of a means of valid cognition (sādhanābhāsa).
The fallacious means of proof has been explained.
Now is the occasion for the refutation;
however, having bypassed that because there is much more to be said, he first speaks regarding perception and inference:
"Furthermore, for the purpose of making oneself understand, there are only two means of valid cognition: perception and inference."
Perception is that which will have its definition stated later, as is inference.
The use of the non-compounded form [of the terms] is for the purpose of indicating that they have distinct objects:
perception has only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.
Inference has only the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object;
the word "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction.
By the phrase "there are only two means of valid cognition," he states the restriction regarding their number.

For indeed, for the Buddhists there are only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). This is because all other means of valid cognition are included within these very two;
and since this inclusion has been discussed in detail in works such as the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, it will not be elaborated upon here.
Now, for the purpose of defining direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he says:
"In that regard, direct perception," and so forth.
The word "in that regard" (*tatra*) has the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
"Direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is the designation of the object to be defined;
"free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) is the definition. This is the distinction between the object to be defined and its definition.
In this context, *pratyakṣa* means that the sense-faculty (*akṣa*) has gone toward [the object].

"Free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*): conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) will have its definition stated later; that from which it is removed—that is, from which it is absent—is "free from conceptual construction."

The summary, the objection, and the rebuttal are as before. "Free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) means either that which is devoid of conceptual construction or that from which conceptual construction has been removed.
The word "that which" (*yat*) is a designation of its essential nature.
And such an object is also a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
He says: knowledge is cognition (*saṃvedana*).
And that [cognition] may also be without an object; therefore, he says: "in regard to an object," meaning in regard to a referent (*viṣaya*).
And that is twofold, due to the distinction between the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, he says:
The meaning is: "in the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form and so forth.

Here, that which was stated as "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) is explained precisely by its own definition as being "devoid of conceptual construction regarding name, genus, and so forth.
It is called *pratyakṣa* because it operates toward each sense faculty (*akṣam akṣam prati*).
In this context, conceptualization of a name is, for example, "Ḍittha";
conceptualization of a genus is, for example, "cow. By the word "etcetera," qualities, actions, and substances are included.
In that regard, the conceptualization of a quality is "white";
the conceptualization of an action is "a cook";
the conceptualization of a substance is "one who has a staff."
It is devoid of these conceptual constructions and devoid of words,
because it has its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its cause.
And it has been said:
For words do not exist within the object, nor are they identical in nature to it, such that when the object appears, they too would appear; and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "that is incapable" and so on:
the word "that" refers back to what was previously indicated.
The *akṣas* are the sense faculties (*indriyas*). Therefore, because it occurs in relation to each and every *akṣa*, that is, in relation to each individual sense faculty, it is called *pratyakṣa*.
He said:

Just as cognition arises through the capacity of the sense faculty, so too does it arise through the capacity of the object; why, then, is it designated by the sense faculty alone and not by the object?
To this it is replied:
because the sense faculty is unique (asādhāraṇa) to that specific cognition, whereas the object is common (sādhāraṇa) to many.
For instance,
the sense faculty is the uncommon cause of its own corresponding sensory consciousness alone,
whereas the object is a common cause, as it is also the object of mental consciousness.
In the world, linguistic designation proceeds by way of what is unique [to a thing], as in the cases of "the sound of a drum" or "a barley sprout.
And it was said by the Bhadanta:
"Because they are the unique causes, they are designated by means of the sense faculties," and so forth.
He says:

"It has been stated that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and so forth are also direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), yet they are not included by this [definition]. How, then, can the definition be all-pervasive (*vyāpin*)? It is replied:

By the statement, "that which is free from conceptual construction is cognition regarding objects such as form," the direct perception of the object is grasped; since this applies without exception even to mental consciousness (*mānasavijñāna*) and so forth, that mental [perception] is indeed included. However, the compound *kalpanāpoḍham* (free from conceptual construction) is used here with reference to worldly perception (*laukikapratyakṣa*).
Enough of this digression.
This is merely a brief summary.
"Anumānam," and so forth. Inference (*anumāna*) is the act of inferring (*anumiti*).
And that is the perception of an object through a mark (*liṅga*); furthermore, the mark has been stated to possess three characteristics (*trirūpa*).
[This refers to] the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth.

Therefore, from a logical mark (*liṅga*) possessing these three forms, there arises a cognition regarding the object to be inferred—a subject (*dharmin*) qualified by a property (*dharma*). What is it like? "There is fire here because of smoke," or "Sound is impermanent because it is produced"—that is inference (*anumāna*).
The two examples, however, are for the purpose of illustrating the two types of reasons known as "effect" (kārya) and "essential nature" (svabhāva), which establish a real entity (vastu).
Now he states the result [of these reasons],
beginning with "In both cases," and so forth.
In both cases— perception and inference—
that very cognition is characterized as perception and inference;
the "result" (phala) is the effect.
Why?
Because it has the nature of realization (*adhigama*).
Realization is discernment; because it has that nature.
For indeed, cognition arises in the very form of a determination;
and there is no other result of cognition apart from that determination,
because they would otherwise reside in different loci.
Much could be said on this point, but enough of this digression;
in any case, there is no distinct result other than those of perception and inference.
He says:
If this were so, it would follow that there is an absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because the two things accepted as existing— perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*)— are [merely] results; and if there is an absence of valid cognition, its result must also be absent.

In that regard, wishing to refute the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: "The status of being a means of valid cognition belongs to that which appears as if possessing an operation. It is "possessing an operation" because it exists together with an operation characterized by the apprehension of an object;
thus, it is understood to be the means of valid cognition.
Because it possesses activity, it is "possessing activity" (*savyāpāravatī*);
it is understood that this refers to "cognition" (*khyāti*).
Thus, that which is both possessing activity and cognition is "active cognition" (*savyāpāravatkhyāti*), meaning perception.
The validity (*prāmāṇya*) belongs to that cognition which possesses an active operation.
This is what is meant:

since it is perceived that knowledge, arising in the form of the object, arises precisely by grasping the object, the aspect of the grasper (*grāhakākāra*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Others, however, explain it as follows: "existent" (sat) refers to the operation (vyāpāra); because it effects the establishment of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), it is called "existent. Since this [cognition] possesses that [operation], it is "possessing an existent operation" (sadyāpāravatī). The remainder is as explained before. Thus, perception (pratyakṣa) and inference (anumāna) have been described.
Now he states what appears as perception [but is not]:
conceptual cognition is that which appears as perception with respect to an object other than its own [referent].
Desiring to explain this very statement of definition, he says:
That cognition which arises for one who conceptualizes "pot" or "cloth," being superimposed with words upon another object— the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—
does not have the particular characteristic (*arthasvalakṣaṇa*) as its object.
The meaning is: because its object is a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, the fallacy of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) has been explained.
Now he states the fallacy of inference (anumānābhāsa):
knowledge preceded by a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa), having a fallacious reason as its cause, is a fallacy of inference,
because of its deviation (vyabhicāra).
He explains this very point:
for fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) have been stated to be of many kinds according to the differences among disputants.

Therefore, that cognition which arises regarding the object of inference—a subject characterized by a property—for one who is unlearned and ignorant of the nature of the "unestablished" (asiddha) and other such fallacies, is a fallacy of inference (anumānābhāsa).
Thus has been explained the fourfold [means of valid cognition], beginning with direct perception.
Now, wishing to state the refutations that remain to be mentioned, he says:
"Refutations (dūṣaṇa) are the pointing out of defects in the proof (sādhana);
the meaning is that they are the making manifest of defects in the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)."
The use of the plural number is because each of these defects, such as the deficiency of the proposition (*pratijñā*), constitutes a fault. These very [faults] are now demonstrated:
the defect of the proof (*sādhanadoṣa*) is its deficiency (*nyūnatva*).
He states the specific [fault] by way of the general:
"The fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) consists in its being contradicted by perception and so forth;
for example, a proposition (*pratijñā*) that is contradicted by perception and so forth."
The fallacies of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) consist in being unestablished (*asiddha*), inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), or contradictory (*viruddha*).

"The reason is unestablished" and so forth [are examples]. Likewise, the fallacies of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*) consist in the non-establishment of the property to be proved (*sādhyadharma*) and so on.
"Exposition of that" means the manifestation of that [fault], such as a reason contradicted by perception, for the purpose of convincing the audience; it does not mean mere exposition.
Regarding "refutation," the singular number is used because it does not exceed the general category of refutation.
The refutation has been stated.
Now he states what constitutes a fallacious refutation (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*):
fallacious refutations are the pointing out of faults in a proof that are non-existent.

Since they point out—that is, reveal—a fault in the proof which is actually non-existent (*abhūta*), meaning it does not exist at all, those are called fallacious refutations consisting of futile rejoinders (*jāti*).
This very point is demonstrated: when the constituent parts of the proof are complete, to state that they are deficient— that is, to say "this is deficient"— is [an instance of] *nyūna*.

The statement "naming a fault in a side that is not defective," and so forth, is established by the literal reading [of the text]. To the question, "What are these fallacious refutations (dūṣaṇābhāsa)?
he says:
For the opposing position is not refuted by these [arguments].
Why?
Because the opposing position is itself faultless.
Thus, the composition of this treatise is concluded.
At the conclusion of the treatise, in order to demonstrate its essential nature, he says:
"merely the categories of things," and so forth.
"Merely the categories of things" refers to the mere enumeration of the terms such as the means of proof (*sādhana*) and so on.
"Explained" means told.
"In the beginning" means first.
"For the sake of establishing a mere direction of reasoning" means for the purpose of establishing just a general orientation of logic.

The reasoning (*yukti*) characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), or the lack of reasoning (*ayukti*) consisting of the various types such as the unestablished (*asiddha*) and so forth,
is to be found elsewhere, in works such as the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*.
The meaning is that it has been well-investigated and determined through conceptual elaboration (*prapañca*).
By whatever merit I have acquired here through explaining the *Nyāyapraveśaka*,
may fortunate beings thereby obtain the bliss of understanding the principles of logic and so forth.
And thus ends this commentary on the *Nyāyapraveśaka*, titled *Śiṣyahitā*.
This is the work of the master Haribhadra.
